2. Appellant is brother's son of the two vendors, Mariam and Alimunnessa, daughters of the recorded owner, late Abbas, who was the appellant's paternal grand father. By two registered sale-deeds dated, 9.5.73 and 10.5.73, Mariam and Alimunnessa sold their shares in the paternal property to the respondents, who are strangers, without serving any notice upon him. He claimed pre-emption by filing Misc. Cases Nos. 121 of 1974 and 174 of 1974 under section 96, State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, in the 1st Court of Munsif, Dhaka. By one sale deed, 1.70-3/4 divided by acres of land was sold for a consideration of Tk. 6000.00, and by the other sale-deed, 1.39-3/4 acres of land was sold for a consideration of Tk.5000.00. His claim was resisted by the pre-emptees on the grounds that the vendors had offered the land to him for purchase but he refused thinking that he would get the land without any price in due course of time and that within his knowledge they took possession of the land, constructed seven dwelling huts, dug a pond, planted trees and made considerable improvement of the land by raising earth. They also took the ground of limitation in that Misc. cases were filed one year after the sale of the land. 

 6. The trial Court, as stated above, refused pre-emption, but on what specific ground, we find it difficult to find out from its judgment. The learned Single' Judge of the High Court Division observed that 'acquiescence and waiver' is implicit in the trial Court's judgment, even though no ground was specifically taken in the written objection of the pre-emptees. Judgment of the trial Court shows that though the plea of "improvement" was taken seven years after the filing of the written objection, there was in fact improvement effected on the land by the pre-emptees, but the pre-emptor's 'deposit' of the improvement cost as well as the consideration of the two sale-deeds was "insufficient". Further, the trial Court found that acts of improvement were done within the knowledge of the pre-emptor. Taking these facts into consideration the learned Single Judge has observed: "the pre-emptees have obviously proved by deposing in the Court and also stating in the written objection that the pre-emptor was offered the sale of the case land by the sellers. It is the finding of the trial Court that the pre-emptor had full know ledge of the improvements made by the pre-emptees. . ... In that view of the matter I cannot help the conclusion that the trial court in effect found a case of acquiescence in favour of the pre-emptees". It is to be seen whether this view of the learned Single Judge is sustainable in law and fact. 

 7. Basis for applying the principles of acquiescence and waiver is found to be the pre-emptor's knowledge of the sale from the very beginning, his refusal to purchase the land when offered and his inaction and silence when many acts of improvements including construction of dwelling huts. Pre-emptor (P.W.1) said that he was not aware of the sale, nor was the land offered to him by the vendors. But the evidence of OPW 1 belies this claim. As to construction of some dwelling huts in the land, it is found have been admitted by PW 1 during cross-examination. OPW 1 --- who is father of one of the purchasers --- has testified that the pre-emptor had even given assurance that he would not claim pre-emption. This statement has been rejected by him. Mr. Nurullah contends that even if the said offer had been made and the appellant refused to purchase and also gave oral assurance that he would not pre-empt, such an assurance would not constitute "acquiescence or waiver" for, the right of pre-emption did not accrue at this stage but it accrued after the sale. In support of this view, he has referred to a decision of the Nagpur High Court in Govinda Marotisa Vs. Ismail, AIR 1950 Nag. 22. In that case, the pre-emptor, when approached by the vendor to purchase the land, not only refused but also gave assurance to the prospective purchaser that he would not exercise his right of pre-emption, but ultimately after the sale he claimed pre-emption. His claim was resisted on the ground of acquiescence and waiver but it was rejected and pre-emption was allowed.
